facts.text: A three-part artificial big toe of wood and leather, dated to about 950 to 710 BC, roughly 3,000 years ago, was found on the foot of a female mummy buried near Luxor.
The toe’s parts were joined so that it could bend, and its signs of wear suggest it was used for walking, not only for appearance.
The Roman Capua leg, made of bronze and wood and dated to about 300 BC, was found in a Roman burial at Capua in southern Italy.
The original Capua leg was destroyed in a bombing raid during the Second World War; only a replica remains.
In the 1500s, European locksmiths, clockmakers and gunsmiths made mechanical hands of iron, brass and wood.
Wearers of these hands used their natural hand to lock the artificial fingers in place and pressed a release button to free them.
The 16th-century French army surgeon Ambroise Paré designed a mechanical hand worked by catches and springs, which a French army captain wore in battle.
Paré also designed an artificial leg with a knee that could be locked for standing and bent at will.
On 3 June 1861, early in the American Civil War, a cannonball shattered the leg of young Confederate soldier James Edward Hanger, and it was amputated.
Frustrated with his peg leg, Hanger spent about three months in his room carving an artificial leg with a bending knee out of barrel staves.
Hanger patented his leg in 1863 and founded a company that still operates today.
Van Phillips lost part of his left leg in a waterskiing accident in 1976.
Phillips based his foot on the hind leg of a cheetah, whose tendon stretches and stores energy when the animal lands.
His carbon foot, sold by the Flex-Foot company he founded in 1984 (the 1980s), compresses like a spring under the wearer’s weight and releases the energy at push-off.
About 90 percent of Paralympic athletes use his design or a variation of it.
Myoelectric arms use electrical signals from the wearer’s muscles to guide battery-powered movement.
Today anyone with a 3D printer can make simple prostheses at home from downloadable files.
